items.content:
Christopher Nolan is the last great director of this century. But not because The Odyssey made $264 million opening weekend.

Because he found a method to irresistible storytelling:

Nolan uses the Plot Map Technique to visualize his storyline.

He doesn’t want “constraints” to hold him back when writing the story (especially if it's complex).

So he uses this technique to help his production team:

1. Visualize the plot arc(s)
2. Create it on screen

Let's take Inception as an example (since I haven't gotten a chance to see The Odyssey yet).

The intricate plot is a journey around dreams within dreams, jumping between layers of reality.

Nolan's Plot Map for Inception resembles Kurt Vonnegut's "Man in Hole" story shape.

This is where the main character:

1. Faces a problem
2. Gets out of it
3. Grows from the experience

But Nolan added an interesting twist:

In Inception, as Cobb (played by DiCaprio) moves closer to the dream world of Limbo, he travels "down" the plot map toward problems.

Then, he must fight his way "up" to reality.

This not only mirrors Cobb's journey but also the movie's core concept of nested dreams.

By using the Plot Map, Nolan keeps the story focused despite the movie's:

• Multiple “dream” storylines
• Competing character arcs
• And ever-increasing stakes

Without the Plot Map, the story would have become unfocused and hard to follow.

Nolan planned the entire 2.5-hour Inception movie on a single page.

Other notable writers have similar practices:

• Norman Mailer (in Harlot's Ghost)
• Henry Miller (in Tropic of Capricorn)
• JK Rowling (in the Harry Potter series)

Want to use this technique for yourself?

Try this:

• Make a Visual Outline (shapes, arrows, visuals)
• Emphasize Key Points (incident, climax, resolution)
• Map Character Development (impact of events/themes)

This will help you keep your story focused while writing.

And then to monetize as a writer ASAP?

items.content:
2 years ago: Afraid of presenting to a 5 person team.

Last week: I spoke at Cannes Lions to 300 CMOs.

After the CMO of LinkedIn, OpenAI, Adobe and JLL.

A couple of years ago, the idea of public speaking would have made me throw up.

I used to get nervous unmuting on a Zoom call.

Last Tuesday, the nerves were still there.
Especially when I saw who was before me...

But I turned those nerves into energy.

I haven't had a personality transplant.
I haven't had public speaking coaching.
I just got tired of letting fear keep me stuck.

So I spent the last 2 years putting myself in uncomfortable situations on purpose.

→ Podcasts and webinars I didn't "feel" ready for
→ Networking events where I knew no one
→ Being in rooms I didn't "belong" in

I've purposefully made myself comfortable with being uncomfortable.

So that when dream situations like this arise…

My first thought isn't "I can't do this?!"

It's "let's f*****g do this."

The nerves never fully go away.

You just learn to use them.


What's something that makes you nervous but you want to do anyway?

items.content:
Most companies rely on one person to post on LinkedIn.

But that one person can only reach one type of buyer.

Let's say you rely on your CEO...

They post on LinkedIn consistently.
They build a loyal audience.

That audience is only one slice of your market.

Instead, you need to tap into your whole company to reach all buyers.

I've been saying this for ages:

Employee-generated content on LinkedIn is the future.

And Clay just proved it.

They generated 6 million LinkedIn impressions last quarter.

Not from ads.
Not from paid partnerships.

From their employees posting (organically!).

They matched each executive to a specific buyer persona:

→ Head of GTM Engineering posts for growth teams
→ Enterprise Sales posts for enterprise buyers
→ Head of Growth posts for marketing leaders
→ Head of Sales posts for revenue leaders
→ Founders post for other founders

Every person owns an audience.
Every post has a job.

Most companies ignore the distribution channel that is right in front of their nose.

Your employees are trusted brand advocates.

We all know the LinkedIn algorithm (and the people on here) prefer humans to logos.

People trust people.
People buy from people.

So start tapping into yours.


Thanks Bruno Estrella for proving my point 🤪  


P.S. I help companies turn their employees into trusted voices on LinkedIn. Comment TEAM if you want to stop relying on one person to reach every buyer.

items.content:
LinkedIn can change your life (it changed mine).

All it takes is 60 minutes a day for a year.

Since posting on LinkedIn:

→ I’ve gained 62,000 followers
→ Spoken on podcasts and at Cannes Lions
→ Built a 6-figure business purely on inbound

You can do the same if you dedicate one hour a day...

And follow my process:

Commenting: 15 mins

→ Pick 10 creators or ideal customers
→ Comment on their posts every day
→ Build relationships and support others

Writing: 15 mins

→ Open Stanley and feed him a prompt
→ One idea, one problem, one lesson
→ A post in your voice in 2 minutes not 2 hours

Responding: 15 mins

→ Never post and ghost
→ Reply to every comment for at least 15 mins
→ Ask follow up questions to build community

Engaging: 15 mins

→ Reply to all new messages
→ Send 10 connection requests per day
→ Send 5 DMs to prospects or people you admire

Bonus: batch your content creation

→ One sitting to write your posts for the week
→ One sitting to create the graphics
→ One sitting to schedule everything out

Stop jumping between tasks because that kills your momentum.

4 blocks.
15 minutes each
4 blocks.
1 year.

Be efficient with your time.
Be consistent.

And, LinkedIn will change your life.


P.S. How long do you spend on LinkedIn? Be honest...

items.content:
I’ve generated 4,601,837 impressions in 12 months.

My viral posts always follow this framework:

I call it the POST framework.

P: Personal story
→ Open with something real and recent
→ Start mid-scene not at the beginning
→ Hook starts with "I" to make it feel human

O: Over-exaggerate the emotion
→ Go harder on the feeling than feels comfortable
→ Amplify how bad it was or how good it became
→ This is where most people hold back → don't

S: Steps they can take
→ What did you actually do next? Make practical
→ 3-8 bullet points works best → use listicles
→ Specific enough that someone can copy it

T: Turn it back to the reader
→ Always end with them, not you
→ Make them feel like the post was written for them
→ End with a question to encourage comments

Here's what it looked like in my best performing post:

P: I applied for 200 jobs & got rejected from them all
O: Depressed, hopeless and no idea what to do next
S: I posted anyway. I was honest. I was vulnerable.
T: This is your sign to post that post

Millions of impressions.
Hundreds of job opportunities.
Thousands of comments and DMs.

All from a four step framework and I stopped fearing honesty.

Try it in your next post.

And, tag me if you do!!


P.S. Do you follow templates or frameworks when writing?

items.content:
What if your Lean system is already too slow for AI-driven manufacturing???

That’s the uncomfortable question behind Industry 4.0.

A lot of factories talk about AI, IoT, Big Data, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing, AR, VR and robots.

The diagram looks clean.

But the floor tells a different story.

Machines still wait for decisions.
Supervisors still chase updates.
Operators still ask what’s next.
Maintenance still reacts after the breakdown.
Quality still finds problems too late.

Then we call it “digital transformation.”

But if the basic system is unstable, technology only makes the instability more visible.

AI can read the data.
IoT can collect the signal.
Cloud can connect the plant.
Robots can repeat the motion.
AR can guide the operator.
Big Data can show the pattern.

But someone still needs to define the process.

What is the standard?
Where is the bottleneck?
Who owns the response?
What happens when the signal turns red?
What decision changes on the floor?

That’s where Lean still matters.

Industry 4.0 without Lean becomes expensive noise.

Lean gives the system structure.
AI makes the system visible.

The real opportunity is not replacing the floor with technology.

It is building a floor where people, process and technology finally speak the same language.

Stability first...
Then AI has something worth reading.
